questions.q: The editorial calls every human being “a book.” What does it say will happen to that book on the Day of Judgement?
options: It will be lost with his death
Not quite. The article says: It will be opened before him, and he will have to read the life he himself has written.
It will be read only by others
Not quite. The article says: It will be opened before him, and he will have to read the life he himself has written.
It will be summarised in a single line
Not quite. The article says: It will be opened before him, and he will have to read the life he himself has written.
It will be opened before him, and he will have to read the life he himself has written
Yes. In his own language, whether he likes it or not.
questions.rationale: “Man will be compelled to read the book he has written. This autobiography of man will be in his own comprehensible language.”

questions.q: What does the editorial call the most serious aspect of this?
options: It is written in haste
Not quite. The article says: There is no second edition – the story cannot be rewritten afterwards.
There is no second edition – the story cannot be rewritten afterwards
Right. The first edition is in our hands now.
Others will add to it
Not quite. The article says: There is no second edition – the story cannot be rewritten afterwards.
The book is very long
Not quite. The article says: There is no second edition – the story cannot be rewritten afterwards.
questions.rationale: “No one will have the opportunity to write a second edition of their life story. Writing the first edition of one’s biography is in the hands of every human being.”

questions.q: “When the prayer is ended, disperse in the land and seek God’s bounty” (62:10). What balance does the article draw from these verses?
options: Trade is to be avoided by the devout
Not quite. The article says: Earning a living is fully allowed, but stays subordinate to one’s duties to God, which take precedence when they call.
Earning a living is fully allowed, but stays subordinate to one’s duties to God, which take precedence when they call
Well read. Then one returns freely to work.
Prayer may be postponed for business
Not quite. The article says: Earning a living is fully allowed, but stays subordinate to one’s duties to God, which take precedence when they call.
Work and worship should never be mixed in one day
Not quite. The article says: Earning a living is fully allowed, but stays subordinate to one’s duties to God, which take precedence when they call.
questions.rationale: “Economic activity is a natural requirement of human existence… However, it is essential that economic activities be subordinated to religious obligations.”

questions.q: Which of these is among the conditions the article sets for a believer’s economic activity?
options: To earn more than his neighbours
Not quite. The article says: To regard what he earns as God’s blessing and to keep within the limits God has set.
To work only for himself
Not quite. The article says: To regard what he earns as God’s blessing and to keep within the limits God has set.
To keep his earnings secret
Not quite. The article says: To regard what he earns as God’s blessing and to keep within the limits God has set.
To regard what he earns as God’s blessing and to keep within the limits God has set
Yes. And to remember God throughout.
questions.rationale: “Earning from economic activities should be considered a blessing of God… Economic activities should not be allowed to cross the limits imposed by God.”

questions.q: Life is full of unpleasant experiences, yet man is asked to be grateful. How, says the article, is that possible?
options: Only through patience – enduring difficulties is what makes thankfulness possible
Well reasoned. The Quran pairs the two.
By waiting for perfect conditions
Not quite. The article says: Only through patience – enduring difficulties is what makes thankfulness possible.
By comparing oneself with the fortunate
Not quite. The article says: Only through patience – enduring difficulties is what makes thankfulness possible.
By ignoring whatever is unpleasant
Not quite. The article says: Only through patience – enduring difficulties is what makes thankfulness possible.
questions.rationale: “It is only when a person patiently endures worldly problems that it becomes possible for him to express his feeling of gratefulness to God.”

questions.q: Why does the article call patience “the superior solution” when facing an adversary?
options: It makes the adversary feel ashamed at once
Not quite. The article says: It keeps one able to think and respond rationally, instead of reacting on impulse.
It wins the sympathy of onlookers
Not quite. The article says: It keeps one able to think and respond rationally, instead of reacting on impulse.
It avoids the need to act at all
Not quite. The article says: It keeps one able to think and respond rationally, instead of reacting on impulse.
It keeps one able to think and respond rationally, instead of reacting on impulse
Correct. Impulse fails; reason succeeds.
questions.rationale: “When he adheres to patience and tolerance, he finds himself competent to make a rational move instead of an impulsive reaction.”

questions.article: Positivity: The Fertile Ground for God-Realization
questions.q: A plant grows only in fertile soil. What does the article name as the soil in which God-realization grows?
options: A quiet village
Not quite. The article says: A positive personality.
A long education
Not quite. The article says: A positive personality.
A wealthy household
Not quite. The article says: A positive personality.
A positive personality
Right. One not ruled by reaction to circumstances.
questions.rationale: “The attainment of God-realization is possible only on the fertile soil of a positive personality.”

questions.article: Positivity: The Fertile Ground for God-Realization
questions.q: How does the article describe a “negative personality”?
options: One who prefers solitude
Not quite. The article says: One who reacts to his surroundings, cannot rise above circumstances, and always looks at the dark side.
One who asks many questions
Not quite. The article says: One who reacts to his surroundings, cannot rise above circumstances, and always looks at the dark side.
One who speaks little
Not quite. The article says: One who reacts to his surroundings, cannot rise above circumstances, and always looks at the dark side.
One who reacts to his surroundings, cannot rise above circumstances, and always looks at the dark side
Yes. Such ground stays barren.
questions.rationale: “A man with a negative personality is one who is of a reactionary disposition. He succumbs to the influence of his environment… He will always look at the negative aspects of events.”

questions.q: Besides being unjust, what two practical harms does the article see in telling only the other side’s faults?
options: It stops a right attitude from developing in oneself, and it leaves the problem unsolved
Exactly. Satisfaction for the teller, no use to anyone.
It takes too long and bores the listener
Not quite. The article says: It stops a right attitude from developing in oneself, and it leaves the problem unsolved.
It is soon forgotten and must be repeated
Not quite. The article says: It stops a right attitude from developing in oneself, and it leaves the problem unsolved.
It makes enemies and costs money
Not quite. The article says: It stops a right attitude from developing in oneself, and it leaves the problem unsolved.
questions.rationale: “There are two disadvantages of such reporting. First, it puts a stop to the development of right attitude, and second, it does not solve the problem.”

questions.q: “Have you considered the water that you drink?… If We so pleased, We certainly could make it salty.” What natural process does the commentary point to?
options: Wells drawing water from rock
Not quite. The article says: Rain as a vast desalination system: pure water rises from the sea and the salt stays behind.
Rain as a vast desalination system: pure water rises from the sea and the salt stays behind
Well read. A reason for gratitude.
Rivers filtering water through sand
Not quite. The article says: Rain as a vast desalination system: pure water rises from the sea and the salt stays behind.
Ice storing water on mountains
Not quite. The article says: Rain as a vast desalination system: pure water rises from the sea and the salt stays behind.
questions.rationale: “When water vapour rises from the sea, pure water rises and the salt is left below. The fact is that the system of rain is a huge universal desalination process.”
